Q: why will Mingw-w64 gcc compiler generate wrong warning about the format of %zd and %a A:

This is an incomplete answer.

The printf function and the formats it support are not implemented by your compiler. They're implemented by the runtime library. In the case of MinGW, the compiler is a version of gcc and the runtime library is, if I'm not mistaken, the one provided by Microsoft for Windows.

The gcc compiler can also warn about printf format strings that it thinks are incorrect, for example if you try to use %s to print an argument of type int. It has to make some assumptions about what the runtime library supports. Typically it just follows the rules of the C standard. But with -std=c11, I'm surprised that it would complain about %zd and %a, which have been valid C since C99. (Some versions of Microsoft's runtime library might not support them, but that shouldn't affect the compile-time behavior.)

The bottom line is that your compiler has decided, for some unknown reason, that it doesn't recognize those formats, but the implementation of printf in the runtime library handles them correctly. There's a mismatch somewhere between your compiler and your runtime library. gcc is probably using some heuristic to guess that certain formats introduced in C99 are not supported, and it's guessing wrong in this case. Perhaps Microsoft updated its runtime library relatively recently and gcc hasn't caught up with the change.

The warnings shouldn't affect the behavior of your program once it's compiled and linked.

Incidentally, the correct format for a size_t value is %zu, not %zd, since size_t is an unsigned type. %zd is likely to work in this case, but use %zu anyway.

I'm able to reproduce the problem with x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc.exe (version 7.4.0) under Cygwin. Removing the -Wall inhibits the warning. [Update, 6 years later: I see the same behavior now with version 13.4.0.]

You can avoid the problem by passing the option -D__USE_MINGW_ANSI_STDIO to gcc. This causes it to use a different implementation for printf.

Q: In CQRS, should my read side return DTOs or ViewModels? A:

it depends on chosen architecture - there's couple of examples:

  1. as of Clean Architecture (in docs: Architecting-Modern-Web-Applications-with-ASP.NET-Core-and-Azure)
  • I would rather use CQRS in Application Layer (between Domain Layer and Presentation Layer) - as you see not DTOs, but ValueObjects are used there (you can apply here some validation logics, but you cannot do it in DTO, though both DTO and ValueObject are the concerns of POCO)... Besides, if you use any ORM (e.g. EF) you can use POCO in either of mentioned ways to transfer data to Presentation Layer (as of what is allowed by chosen Web Application),
  1. as of CQRS with DDD pattern - example in Onion arch description - CQRS looks like this and CQRS by its own of course lacks some transportation logics to endpoints, because you should follow the SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) - you should return ONLY the result of your Query.
  • Therefore sometimes it is used with DDD patten (for write ops.), Because in DDD you can have separate DBs for read & write contexts (and only on server they will communicate with each other e.g. using Event-Driven Pattern)...
  • or with EDA
  • or Even the simpliest use of CQRS with Event Sourcing requires both query and queryHandler: query was sent from GUI, queryHandler process query (as on given above image), executing Task e.g. GetByGroup and returns ONLY ListOfRecords to Controller, each of them is defined in DTO (just as definition of transferred struct). But the final goal of Controller is to return View (if you use old monolite MVC pattern)
  • In WPF you can return result of query to ViewModel and refresh xaml-View,
  • in WebApplication (it depends on WebAPI) - e.g. in Blazor - your Views (.razor files) are already registered and queryHandler can act as Event_Handler to update your projection to Page.razor in Vertical-Slicing Architecture. Just investigate your project in Blazor template of VisualStudio. And use MediatR framework for your CQRS pattern - you will not tnink anymore about DTOs, ValueObjects, IAsyncResults, and will do only modern Task-based application!
  • in microservice architectore (docs: NET-Microservices-Architecture-for-Containerized-NET-Applications) we also see in description, that

The application layer can be the Web API itself. The important design aspect here is that the microservice has split the queries and ViewModels (data models especially created for the client applications) from the commands, domain model, and transactions following the CQRS pattern. This approach keeps the queries independent from restrictions and constraints coming from DDD patterns that only make sense for transactions and updates, as explained in later sections.

Q: Concurrent update error: race condition error in FastAPI A:

There is no single answer to this question: the solution will depend on what kind of updates are being applied, and what are the constraints under which the application is operating,

In this case, it seems you have a single table with two columns which are frequently being updated leading to concurrent update errors. One way to handle this might be two move the two columns to a separate table, and insert each new status into this table rather than updating a single row. Since you are now doing only INSERTs instead of UPDATEs you will no longer get concurrent updates. Of course the trade-off is that now you must query the table to get the latest status, and you must devise a way to clear down old records periodically to prevent the table from growing too large.

Since you are using SQLAlchemy you can do some magic to create a relationship that will fetch the latest status for a task (note that it is read-only: new statuses must be appended to the tasks statuses attribute.

import datetime as dt

import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy import orm
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(orm.DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class TaskStatus(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'task_statuses'

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    status: Mapped[str]
    update_time: Mapped[dt.datetime]
    task_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(sa.ForeignKey('tasks.id'))

    task: Mapped['Task'] = orm.relationship('Task', back_populates='statuses')


class Task(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'tasks'

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    statuses: Mapped[list['TaskStatus']] = orm.relationship('TaskStatus', back_populates='task')

    @orm.declared_attr
    def __mapper_args__(cls) -> dict:
        statuses = TaskStatus.__table__
        most_recent_child = (
            sa.select(statuses.c.id)
            .where(statuses.c.task_id == cls.id)
            .order_by(statuses.c.update_time.desc())
            .limit(1)
            .correlate(cls.__table__)
            .scalar_subquery()
        )

        rel: Mapped[TaskStatus] = orm.relationship(
            TaskStatus,
            primaryjoin=sa.and_(
                TaskStatus.id == most_recent_child, TaskStatus.task_id == cls.id
            ),
            uselist=False,
            viewonly=True,
        )
        return {'properties': {'latest_status': rel}}


engine = sa.create_engine('sqlite://', echo=True)
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
Session = orm.sessionmaker(engine)

with Session.begin() as s:
    task = Task()
    s.add(task)
    for status in ['first', 'second', 'third']:
        ts = TaskStatus(status=status, update_time=dt.datetime.now())
        task.statuses.append(ts)

with Session() as s:
    task = s.scalar(sa.select(Task))
    assert task.latest_status.status == 'third'

    task.statuses.append(TaskStatus(status='fourth', update_time=dt.datetime.now()))

    s.commit()

    assert len(task.statuses) == 4
    assert task.latest_status.status == 'fourth'

Q: Set environment variables from file of key/value pairs A:

This is what i use at moment:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0
# /usr/local/bin/parse-env-file

# This function filters out any lines that do not contain a variable assignment, and trims any comments at the end.
function filter_var_assignments() {
    sed -nE 's/^\s*([[:alpha:]_][[:alnum:]_]*)\s*=\s*(.[^#]*)(#.*)?$/\1 = \2/p'
}
# This function imports variable assignments from stdin, and sets them as r/o global variables.
function import_vars() {
    local var _ value
    while read -r var _ value; do
        # Check if the value is an array assignment.
        if test "${value:0:1}${value: -1}" == "()"; then
            # Remove the leading and trailing parentheses, and split the value into an array.
            # shellcheck disable=SC2162,SC2229
            read -a "${var}" <<<"${value:1:-1}" 2>/dev/null || continue
            # Set as r/o array
            typeset -garx "$var" 2>/dev/null
        else
            # Set as r/o string
            declare -grx "$var"="$value" 2>/dev/null || continue
        fi
        imported_vars+=("$var")
    done < <(filter_var_assignments)
    # typeset -p "${imported_vars[@]}"
}

function main() {
    local -a imported_vars
    local declare_output

    if test $# -gt 0; then
        for f in "$@"; do
            import_vars < "$f"
        done
    else
        import_vars <<-EOF
            test1=val1
            test2=val2#comment
            test3 = val3# comment
            test4 = val4 # comment
            #test5 = val5
            ;test6 = val6
            function test7(){} # comment
            function test8(){
                test9=val9
            } # comment
            test10=(val10 val11 val12)
        EOF
    fi

    for v in "${imported_vars[@]}"; do
        # Use declare -p to get the variable's declaration
        declare_output="$(declare -p "$v" 2>/dev/null)"
        printf "Imported: %s => %s\n" "${v}" "${declare_output#*=}"
    done
}

main "$@"
  • Pro's:
    • Filters out any line that is not a variable assignment.
    • Trims comments at end of lines.
    • Supports Array assignments.
    • Creates global read-only exported variables.
    • Ability to protect vs changing certain variables by making those variables r/o before importing. (Can remove the r/o flag again after importing)
  • Con's:
    • Uses sed for filtering.

Example run:

❯  parse-env-file
Imported: test1 => "val1"
Imported: test2 => "val2"
Imported: test3 => "val3"
Imported: test4 => "val4"
Imported: test9 => "val9"
Imported: test10 => ([0]="val10" [1]="val11" [2]="val12")
  • To read from a file, instead of the build-in test data, just add the file name(s) after the script name on the command-line.
